title: Access models in the roadmap's nouns
objective: Decide which reads the roadmap's sharing rule allows on a small world, and tell role-based, attribute-based and relationship-based rules apart.

blocks.md: Your system now has tenants, teams, users, roles, documents and sharing. The roadmap states the read rule in one sentence: a user may see a document when they are a team member or it is explicitly shared. Whatever no rule allows is denied.

choice.prompt: frank is in Acme, on Growth. q3-plan belongs to Payments, also in Acme, and nobody has shared it with him. Under the roadmap's rule, in a system that denies by default, can frank see q3-plan?

options.text: Yes: nothing in the rule forbids it.
options.why: A default-deny system allows exactly what some rule derives.

options.text: No: neither way in applies to him.
options.why: He is not on Payments and holds no share.

options.text: Yes: he and Payments share a tenant.
options.why: No rule mentions tenants, so sharing one grants nothing.

segments.title: Reading a rule on a world

blocks.md:
A policy here is facts and rules. A fact records one relationship: a membership, an owner, a share. A rule says when a new fact follows from others. The engine derives every fact the rules allow and nothing else, which is default deny. A premise written `!revoked(d, u)` must be absent.

Rules differ in what they consult. A role-based rule asks what you are: admins may delete. An attribute-based rule compares properties: clearance at or above the label. A relationship-based rule follows a path through the data, from user to team to document. The roadmap's rule is relationship-based, and it has three ways in.[^1]

[^1]: In Zanzibar the recursion in such paths lives in the engine, in Cedar in the data (each entity carries its ancestors), and in Datalog in the rules. S7.L3 shows why that matters to a checker.

The toy below relates users straight to documents. Make your call before you run it.

blocks.direction: Query asks: is `canread(1, 4)` derivable? `sat` means yes, so user 1 may read document 4.

code.text:
.decl member(u: number, d: number)
.decl shared(u: number, d: number)
.decl revoked(u: number, d: number)
.decl canread(u: number, d: number)
.output canread

member(1, 3).
shared(1, 4).
revoked(1, 4).

canread(u, d) :- member(u, d).
canread(u, d) :- shared(u, d), !revoked(u, d).

call.prompt: What does the engine answer for `canread(1, 4)`?

options.why: `shared(1, 4)` is one premise, and rule 2 also needs `revoked(1, 4)` absent.
Rule 1 needs `member(1, 4)`, and rule 2's negated premise fails.
A program with negation over finitely many facts reaches its fixpoint in finitely many steps.

blocks.after: In Datalog, `sat` means derivable, which here means allowed. In S1, after you asserted a negation, `sat` meant a violation existed. Read the polarity each time.

blocks.md: The roadmap's world, W0, adds teams, owners and tenants. Its rules are the three ways in.

blocks.direction: Query asks: which (user, document) pairs are derivable? The cell prints `canread` as a matrix of users and documents.

code.text:
.decl tenant_of_team(t: symbol, a: symbol)
.decl tenant_of_user(u: symbol, a: symbol)
.decl member(u: symbol, t: symbol, r: symbol)
.decl owns(t: symbol, d: symbol)
.decl share_user(d: symbol, u: symbol)
.decl share_team(d: symbol, t: symbol)
.decl revoked(d: symbol, u: symbol)
.decl canread(u: symbol, d: symbol)
.output canread

// the world: two tenants, three teams, four users, four documents
tenant_of_team("payments", "acme").  tenant_of_team("growth", "acme").  tenant_of_team("legal", "birch").
tenant_of_user("dana", "acme").  tenant_of_user("frank", "acme").
tenant_of_user("gia", "birch").  tenant_of_user("hal", "birch").
member("dana", "payments", "editor").  member("frank", "growth", "viewer").
member("gia", "legal", "admin").       member("hal", "legal", "viewer").
owns("payments", "q3-plan").  owns("growth", "roadmap").
owns("legal", "contract").    owns("legal", "layoffs-memo").
share_user("contract", "dana").
share_team("roadmap", "payments").

// rule 1: a member of the owning team
canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, _), owns(t, d).
// rule 2: shared with the user, and not revoked
canread(u, d) :- share_user(d, u), !revoked(d, u).
// rule 3: shared with one of the user's teams
canread(u, d) :- member(u, t, _), share_team(d, t).

call.prompt: dana is in Acme. contract belongs to Birch. Can dana read contract?

options.why: Rule 2 fires on `share_user("contract", "dana")`, and no rule mentions tenants.
Tenants are not walls, and Birch chose to share contract.

blocks.after: Your system will need exactly this: a document that crosses a tenant on purpose. S7.L7 comes back to it.

choice.prompt: Edit the program: Birch revokes dana's share of contract, and shares layoffs-memo with Growth. Which statement is true?

options.text: dana can still read contract, because it is shared with her.
options.why: Rule 2 also needs the revocation absent, and it is now present.

options.text: frank can read q3-plan, because no rule forbids it.
options.why: Whatever no rule derives is denied.

options.text: frank can read layoffs-memo, a Birch document.
options.why: Rule 3 applies: layoffs-memo is shared with Growth, and frank is on Growth.

options.text: No Acme user can read a Birch document, because tenants are walls.
options.why: The share to Growth crosses the tenant boundary, as the share to dana did.

choice.prompt: Which of these rules is relationship-based?

options.why: It consults a role and nothing else, so it is role-based.

options.text: A user may read a document whose label is at or below their clearance.
options.why: It compares properties of the user and the document, so it is attribute-based.

options.text: A user may read a document shared with any team they belong to.
options.why: It follows a path from user to team to document, as rule 3 does.

blocks.title: Twin
blocks.md: Zanzibar writes rule 3 as `doc:readme#viewer@group:eng#member`: members of group:eng are viewers of doc:readme. See section 2.1 of the [Zanzibar paper](https://www.usenix.org/conference/atc19/presentation/pang) (read 2026-10-23). The paper describes a closed system, so there is no commit to pin.

The bench image is a local build (statespace-bench, built from bench/image/Dockerfile on 2026-10-26); its digest is the manifest list's and it was never pushed. binary_sha256 equals RUN-souffle-version's.
Souffle warns on stderr "No rules/facts defined for relation revoked" for every program that declares revoked without facts; the warning does not change the exit code (0).

Provenance: Souffle labels the share_user rule (R3) in its proof output; the lessons call it rule 2. For canread("frank", "contract") it prints "Tuple not found": no derivation tree exists for a denied cell. The tree shows only the positive premise; the negated premise !revoked is not printed as a node.
S7.L3 cell 3: violation holds in w4 and w6, and wf2_broken holds in exactly w4 and w6, so with WF2 imposed no violation remains within the eight-world scope.
